title: Freenet — Clarke at FUTO
subtitle: Ian Clarke's update on Freenet: with Western governments now arresting posters and quietly tuning recommendation algorithms, the fix is structural — kill the servers, run every app on a self-organizing peer network where the code governing shared state is public and nobody, including its author, can take anything down.

footnotes: 52-minute update talk by Ian Clarke ("sanity" online), hosted by FUTO, followed by ~7 minutes of Q&A. Positioned as a progress report on the rewritten Freenet, not an architecture deep-dive — Clarke points to his February talk ("Freenet lives") for the mechanics.

Pre-alpha and design-stage: Freenet Mail (email-like), Raven (a decentralized social feed), Harvest (a decentralized Etsy). Clarke is explicit that the point is not to beat the incumbents but to demonstrate that every critical use case can be built decentralized and stay convenient.
Q&A — why River before Mail: group chat is useful among four or five friends, email only works if it's pervasive. Chat scales down as well as up; "two people on a social network" is not interesting.

Q&A — capability stratification: the contract's own WASM code decides who may write (River requires messages signed by an authorized member); restricting reads is done by encrypting, which is exactly how private rooms work.

Q&A — team and traction: Clarke full-time, two part-time developers in Spain, a volunteer community around them, hundreds of newcomers a day in the River rooms. Claude Code skills now encode the complexity of building a Freenet app, so contributors ship without knowing Rust. Harvest payments stay mechanism-agnostic — expected to be crypto via a vendor's own address, with no ZP-style currency of their own.

ZP resonance (my framing, not Clarke's): contracts/delegates map almost one-to-one onto the chain/vault split — shared state carrying its own governing code, private material never leaving hardware the operator controls, and a delegate that signs on request rather than surrendering the key is precisely the singular-sovereign-root posture. The auditable-contract argument is *signing is gravity* aimed at recommendation engines, and "nobody runs the network" is P3 *there is no center* stated as a threat model. The instructive divergence: Freenet has no operator ceremony — no equivalent of P9's *the system acts; the operator signs* — so its trust story ends at transparency where ZP's continues into authority.
